interactions.summary: Jiang answers the paradox of divine punishment by staging a parent-and-addict analogy: real love may require letting someone hit rock bottom so that harm stops and recovery becomes possible.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Student question answered through Jiang-led analogy

speaker_notes.note: This is a real student question that asks Jiang to reconcile divine love with punishment.
The Good Samaritan comparison is imprecise but functionally supports Jiang's distinction between help and enabling.

claims.claim: Jiang rejects the idea that divine catastrophe is just God showing humanity something; he insists the problem is punishment, not pedagogy alone.
Jiang's analogy is that a loved one addicted to drugs may need forceful intervention, even jail or abandonment, because permissive help can preserve the destructive pattern.
For Jiang, love means wanting the best possible life for someone, not merely shielding them from pain.
Jiang says the logic of divine retribution is that society may need to hit rock bottom before it can recognize and repair its corruption.

signature_moments.moment: Love is redefined as forcing reality on someone who can no longer live well without it.
signature_moments.source_phrase: let him or her hit rock bottom
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is Jiang's strongest answer to the mercy-versus-punishment paradox and drives his reading of catastrophe as severe love.

signature_moments.moment: A civilization may need to collapse far enough to see its own sickness.
signature_moments.source_phrase: humanity has to reach rock bottom
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It scales the family analogy up to plague, judgment, and the political meaning of Inferno.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang's explanation for why punishment can be an expression of love: degradation becomes the precondition for recovery.

chronology_notes.note: This packet resolves the theological paradox introduced at the end of the prior packet, moving the lecture from historical framing into Jiang's substantive theory of judgment.

uncertainty_notes.note: The student's biblical example is ASR-distorted, but Jiang clearly uses it as an instance of the difference between enabling and forcing moral recognition.
